items.title: A Multi-Stakeholder Survey Examining Incident Review Processes in a National Healthcare System: A Study Protocol
items.abstract: Background Incident reporting is central to patient safety, yet translating review findings into systemic learning remains challenging. Within the Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) 2020 Incident Management Framework (IMF), Improvement Planning and Monitoring (Step 6) is where findings are intended to become service change. How well reviews achieve this, and how the review methodologies in use shape that performance, has not been systematically examined. This protocol sets out a study examining how these methodologies operate in practice and the perceived quality of the recommendations they produce, by capturing the accounts of multiple stakeholders linked to the same reviews, with particular attention to human factors in the transition from learning to action. Methods The study uses a cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey design. A stratified random sample of 96 incident reviews will be drawn from the National Incident Management System (NIMS): 48 Category 1 (major/severe harm) and 48 Category 2 (moderate harm), equally divided between acute and community settings. Seven role-tailored instruments, mapped to four stakeholder categories (reviewers and commissioners; clinical staff; implementers; patients, service users and families), combine rating-scale and written-response questions organised around the six IMF principles. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive and non-parametric methods, qualitative data using reflexive thematic analysis, and the two strands integrated through joint displays. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been granted by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Trinity College Dublin and the HSE National Research Ethics Committee. A pilot phase of five reviews will precede national administration. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentation, and a summary report to the HSE, and are intended to identify systemic barriers to improvement planning and inform a national logic model for shared learning.

items.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Software Factory with Human Oversight
items.abstract: ZenoFCIS is a neuro symbolic software factory that adheres to the principles of formally verified functional core, imperative shell. The overeer who in most cases is human, communicates with an LLM that translates their intent into ZAL, the Zeno Abstraction Language. From here, the intent becomes a behavioral contract which can be directly synthesized by program synthesis. The human is supported by a multi agent team which includes LLMs, and the process utilizes neuro symbolic feedback loops to produce high assurance software.

items.title: A New Frontier in the Digital Divide? Toward a Nuanced Understanding of Internet Unadopters
items.abstract: Conventionally, digital divide research focuses on people who have never used the internet (nonadopters). However, those who formerly adopted the internet but no longer use it (unadopters) are often neglected. Analysis of the 2016 and 2018 waves of the China Family Panel Studies reveals that the likelihood of internet unadoption in China increases with advancing age, decreasing income, and lower educational attainment. Those who are disadvantaged at the adoption stage are less likely to remain online later. In addition, the device divide is positively related to persistent internet use. Moreover, behavioral habitual use mediates the influence of perceived importance on internet unadoption and becomes a substantively important predictor of internet unadoption behavior. These findings validate the relevance of conventional user-focused digital divide initiatives, originally designed for nonadopters, in addressing the challenge of unadoption.

items.title: A paradigm shift toward explainable and federated intelligence for brain tumor MRI analysis
items.abstract: Deep learning techniques in brain tumor analysis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans have improved significantly, but their clinical deployment is limited by models with limited interpretability (‘black-box' models) and data privacy limitations. This paper analyses recent literature and aims to explore the intersection of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Federated Learning (FL). Following the PRISMA protocol, a systematic search was conducted in Scopus on February 24, 2026, covering English-language journal articles and conference proceedings published from January 2020 to February 2026. The search initially identified 767 records, which were screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria for MRI-based brain tumor studies addressing deep learning, explainability, privacy, or Federated Learning, resulting in 147 initially retained studies for the final screening set. One study was subsequently identified as formally retracted and excluded from the final synthesis, resulting in 146 included studies. The review classifies the literature into five primary research themes in brain tumor analysis: explainability, deep learning frameworks, privacy-preserving learning, advanced architectures (Transformers and Mamba), and multimodal learning. The literature suggests a paradigm shift in brain tumor analysis toward model interpretability using XAI. However, there is a significant knowledge gap in privacy-preserving collaborative learning models. Advanced architectures are proposed to solve brain tumor problems, but there are still limitations in model generalization, computational costs, and clinical reliability.

items.title: A Prescriptive Design Framework for CRM-Integrated Agentic AI in Hospital Patient Services: Design Science Development and Empirical Proof-of-Concept Evaluation
items.abstract: Hospital patient services (registration and appointment scheduling) often face fragmented systems, long handling times, and data-entry errors, while patients expect instant 24/7 digital interactions. This study uses Design Science Research to develop a prescriptive five-phase framework for CRM-integrated agentic AI, whose novelty lies in combining bounded transactional agency, middleware-mediated access to CRM/SIMRS tools, and staged governance. Its design assumptions are evaluated through a controlled proof of concept (PoC). The PoC implements an end-to-end transactional conversational workflow (WhatsApp/web chat) in which an LLM-based agent uses API middleware to call tools on a CRM/SIMRS sandbox, avoiding direct database access. The artefact structures are: preparation and alignment; analysis and detailed design; implementation and controlled testing; pilot and evaluation; and scaling and institutionalization, supported by governance mechanisms (clinical “green/red” boundaries, audit logging, and human-in-the-loop supervision). Empirical evaluation applied black-box testing across 15 positive and negative scenarios comprising 285 executions. Of these, 246 met the predefined scenario criteria, and 39 failed, yielding an overall controlled-scenario success rate of 86.32%. A separate message-level latency log contained 292 message-response pairs across 58 recorded conversation groups; median response time was 9 s (IQR 4–19 s), with 88.70% of responses returned in under 30 s and 97.26% in under 60 s. Selected persisted CRM records were additionally checked through authorized visual inspection, with no discrepancies observed. These findings support technical feasibility under controlled PoC conditions while identifying patient-centred evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, production load testing, economic evaluation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-site validation as requirements for broader deployment.

items.title: A psychological prediction automatic reasoning framework for explaining potential cognitive states
items.abstract: Psychological prediction, the ability to infer human behavior and intentions, is essential for artificial intelligence and human–machine interaction. Existing deep learning models often rely on surface-level fitting and lack structured abductive interpretability, while traditional neuro-symbolic systems suffer from non-differentiable discontinuities and limited adaptability to dynamic contextual constraints. This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic automated reasoning framework for modeling latent cognitive states under contextual constraints. The framework introduces a context-aware adaptive SMC resampling operator (CAR-SMC), which uses energy-based penalties to filter hypotheses violating contextual constraints. We further design an executable differentiable program synthesis (EDPS) module and a hybrid iterative program–cognition interaction (HIPCI) mechanism. Through stop-gradient-based directional optimization, HIPCI separates the update pathways of belief and program representations during alternating fixed-point optimization, reducing circular gradient entanglement. Experiments on OpenToM and FANToM show that the framework improves the abductive consistency rate (ACR), an empirical belief–action consistency metric, to 70.8% and 52.1%, respectively. Under the adopted classification-oriented evaluation setup, these results indicate additional ACR gains over pure fine-tuned encoder classifiers and higher ACR than the evaluated few-shot ToT reference baseline (~ 7B), while using fewer parameters and maintaining an average inference latency of 215 ms per instance. Overall, this work provides a differentiable framework for machine Theory of Mind with process-level structural interpretability under the evaluated text-based classification setting.

items.title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets
items.abstract: Abstract The European Law Institute’s Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a right for consumers to use digital assistants in business-to-consumer relations. The DACC’s definition encompasses consumer AI agents (CAIAs), which use AI-generated outputs to determine transactionally relevant matters left open by consumers and initiate or perform transactional actions. The article examines two concerns. First, recognition and safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, causing consumers to overestimate CAIAs’ technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic markets, disproportionately benefit incumbents in adjacent digital markets, and foster concentration, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. Legislation should therefore first establish essential rules governing delegation, responsibility and market contestability. Technical implementation may be entrusted to European standardisation bodies, but the Commission’s request should define tasks precisely and maximise transparency and balanced stakeholder participation to mitigate legitimacy concerns. Only once CAIAs are sufficiently reliable and the legal framework more mature should the right to use a CAIA be recognised.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Analysis of AI-Driven Legacy System Modernization in the Public Sector
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper examines the socio-technical limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize legacy information systems in the public sector, where continuity of services, policy obligations, security, and public accountability shape technology decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The paper combines a review of literature on public-sector AI adoption and legacy-system modernization with an anonymous survey of more than 50 public-sector technology professionals. Participants represented technical, analytical, management, application-support, and project roles and a range of professional experience. Survey topics included AI benefits and risks, organizational readiness, security and privacy, governance, workforce challenges, and human oversight. Findings: Respondents recognized AI's potential to support modernization but raised concerns about citizen-data protection, compliance, trust in generated outputs, integration, workforce readiness, and accountability. The findings suggest that AI should augment, not replace, experienced professionals and established engineering controls. Survey responses also point to the importance of governance, training, secure environments, phased implementation, and human validation. Originality: The paper brings technical, organizational, institutional, and ethical constraints together in a public-sector legacy-modernization context. It emphasizes that AI should augment, rather than replace, accountable human expertise and that successful adoption depends on governance, secure data practices, validation, and organizational readiness. Research limitations/implications: The survey reflects the views of its participants and should not be treated as representative of all public-sector technology professionals. Environmental impacts were not directly measured in the structured survey. Further research could test these findings across agencies and modernization projects.

items.title: A sparse autoencoder and explainable machine learning framework for provenance tracing of historic blue bricks in architectural conservation
items.abstract: Provenance identification of historic blue bricks supports material authenticity in architectural conservation, but missing inscriptions and incomplete archives limit conventional approaches. We integrate sparse autoencoders, machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence to classify brick provenance using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence data. Spectral latent features are fused with elemental concentrations, and synthetic minority oversampling addresses class imbalance. In a dataset of 52 bricks from five regions, the random forest classifier achieved 95% test accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.973. Shapley additive explanations identified Rb, Al and Zr as important discriminative variables, while decoder-based analysis linked latent features to mineral phases. Ablation and feature-substitution analyses indicated complementary elemental and spectral information. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a high-accuracy and theoretically interpretable engineering solution for the provenance identification of historic blue bricks.

items.title: A Survey of Explainable Reinforcement Learning: Targets, Methods and Needs
items.abstract: The success of recent Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has been accompanied by the opacity of their internal mechanisms, due notably to the use of deep neural networks. In order to understand these internal mechanisms and explain the output of these AI models, a set of methods have been proposed, grouped under the domain of eXplainable AI (XAI). This paper focuses on a sub-domain of XAI, called eXplainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), which aims to explain the actions of an agent that has learned by reinforcement learning. We propose an intuitive taxonomy based on two questions ‘What’ and ‘How’. The first question focuses on the target that the method explains, while the second relates to the way the explanation is provided. We use this taxonomy to provide a state-of-the-art review of over 250 papers. In addition, we present a set of domains close to XRL, which we believe should get attention from the community. Finally, we identify some needs for the field of XRL.

items.title: A systematic literature review of generative AI support for pre-service teachers in designing computational thinking instruction
items.abstract: Abstract Computational Thinking (CT) is increasingly expected across curricula, yet pre-service teachers often report limited preparation for translating CT concepts into instructional practice. This systematic literature review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) supports pre-service teachers’ instructional design and what the available evidence implies for CT-oriented teaching. Using the PRISMA approach, the review synthesised 26 empirical studies identified through Scopus and ScienceDirect under the original eligibility criteria. The evidence base was heterogeneous: only two studies were coded as explicitly addressing CT integration, fifteen as implicitly CT-aligned, and nine as having no identifiable CT integration. Accordingly, indirect studies are treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of CT instructional design. Across the literature, GenAI was used for ideation, lesson planning, feedback, multimedia generation, and iterative refinement. Several studies reported gains or positive experiences in efficiency, confidence, engagement, creativity, or instructional design competence; however, these outcomes were study-specific and should not be generalised as improvements in CT competence. Several studies have linked more productive use of GenAI to human evaluation, AI literacy, pedagogical or subject-matter knowledge, and structured frameworks or training. Reported risks included inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, hallucinations, overreliance, metacognitive laziness, and ethical concerns. Because the search was limited to Scopus and ScienceDirect and applied an open-access criterion, the review may be affected by database and accessibility bias. Overall, direct evidence that GenAI improves CT-specific instructional design remains preliminary; the broader literature more strongly supports a conditional role for GenAI as a pedagogical scaffold in CT-relevant instructional design.

items.title: A Topology-Guided GeoAI Agentic Framework for Urban Flood Screening
items.abstract: Open-world geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) agents can transform public geospatial data into accessible decision support for real-world challenges, but must balance autonomous reasoning with reliable spatial analysis and human oversight. We present a topology-guided GeoAI agentic framework for urban flood screening that takes a place name, drawn region, or uploaded boundary and returns ranked candidate basins with an interactive map and report. A deterministic controller retrieves public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure layers, extracts terrain depressions with discrete Morse theory, and ranks basins with a relative flood-priority score. The language model acts only at recorded decision points: selecting a persistence threshold from a precomputed candidate table, drafting recommendations from computed evidence, and reviewing each recommendation against the same evidence. Three human-in-the-loop checkpoints let users revise the threshold, factor weights, or recommendation. In a College Park, Maryland case study, the selected threshold reduced 278 raw terrain minima to 70 basins, with 77% of these basins' lowest points also identified as sinks by a separately computed eight-direction (D8) flow-routing model. Across four further study areas, agreement ranged from 61% to 83%. items.title: ABRA: Agent-Bound UI for Human-Agent Communication beyond Chat with Reusable Views
items.abstract: Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent-Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task-specific meanings. Agents bind task-specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework-agnostic prototype of Agent-Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM-backed agents on canvas authoring, owner-side consequence resolution, and cross-agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.

items.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses
items.abstract: AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.

items.title: Academic-year differences and psychophysiological associations with objective spinal parameters in physiotherapy students: a cross-sectional DIERS formetric 4D study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physiotherapy students are exposed to differing physical and psychological demands across classroom-based and clinical stages of training. Although musculoskeletal symptoms, stress, sleep quality and burnout have been widely investigated in healthcare students, these factors have rarely been examined together using objective three-dimensional spinal assessment. This study compared spinal parameters between third- and fourth-year physiotherapy students and examined their associations with academic-year-related physical exposure, psychophysiological factors, sleep quality, and physical activity. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 132 healthy physiotherapy students (70 third year and 62 fourth year) underwent three-dimensional spinal assessment using the DIERS Formetric 4D system. Trunk length, kyphotic angle and lordotic angle were recorded. Sleep quality, anxiety, burnout and physical activity were evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, Maslach Burnout Inventory and International Physical Activity Questionnaire. Group comparisons were performed, followed by hierarchical multiple linear regression analyses to examine independent associations and bootstrap mediation analyses to explore indirect associations. Multivariable analyses were adjusted for relevant anthropometric, academic-year, school-based standing and sitting, and physical activity variables. RESULTS: Fourth-year students reported longer school-based standing and shorter sitting durations than third-year students (both p < 0.001), alongside lower trait anxiety and burnout scores and higher walking activity. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed in trunk length, kyphotic angle, or lordotic angle; kyphotic angle was numerically lower in fourth-year students but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.051). In the fully adjusted hierarchical model, trait anxiety (β = - 0.148, p = 0.022) and poorer sleep quality (PSQI; β = - 0.139, p = 0.032) were independently associated with shorter trunk length, whereas academic-year group and school-based standing and sitting durations were not. The final model explained 68.4% of trunk-length variance. Exploratory mediation analysis identified a significant indirect association between emotional exhaustion and trunk length through sleep quality (B = - 0.300, 95% bootstrap CI - 0.686 to - 0.062, p = 0.048), while the corresponding direct and total associations were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: Objective spinal parameters did not differ significantly between third- and fourth-year physiotherapy students despite marked differences in their school-based standing and sitting exposure. Trunk length was independently associated with trait anxiety and sleep quality after multivariable adjustment, while exploratory analysis identified an indirect association between emotional exhaustion and trunk length through sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than temporal or causal relationships. Collectively, the results highlight the potential value of educational strategies that extend beyond ergonomic considerations to integrate biomechanical, psychological, and recovery-related factors during physiotherapy training. items.title: Accuracy and Efficiency of Articicial Intelligence Tools for Transcription in Qualitative Research
items.abstract: Verbatim transcription in qualitative research is hugely time consuming, yet critical for data validity. The rise in artificial intelligence tools for transcription provides new opportunities for researchers. We assessed the accuracy and efficiency of two widely accessible AI tools and human transcription to provide empirical guidance for researchers. We compared 10 verbatim transcripts generated via three transcription modes: human, Otter.ai and MAXQDA. We compared transcription time, cost, errors (volume and type), and correction time. Results show that the AI tools were highly time/cost efficient but had 2-3 times more errors than human transcription. Accounting for average correction time, AI tools generated a transcript in 1.25 - 2.5 hours for USD31-38 per transcript; thus 3–6 times faster and 3 times cheaper than human transcription. However, human review of AI transcription remains critical for data validity; thus, AI tools can assist in the transcription process versus generating the final product. We develop recommendations for each phase of the research process to maximize the benefits of using AI transcription tools.

items.title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
items.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

items.title: Adoption and Impacts of a Socratic Generative AI Tutor in Undergraduate Algebra
items.abstract: Instructors looking to support personalized mathematics learning may provide access to generative AI tutoring tools. Few studies explore the effectiveness of these systems in classroom settings. This is particularly important in mathematics, where genAI is a shift from historic adaptive intelligent tutoring systems. We evaluated undergraduate algebra students’ (n=58) use of the Socratic generative AI tutor, Khanmigo, through a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study using survey, registrar, grades, and software usage data. One course section was assigned four Khanmigo activities throughout the semester (experimental), while the other was provided access and an introductory activity only (control). A Wilcoxon Rank Sum test showed that experimental students engaged in significantly more chats than control students (p<0.05), controlling for in-class activities. Instrumental help seeking was positively correlated with Khanmigo use, while intentions of seeking help from technology sources were negatively correlated with use. Khanmigo use did significantly predict mathematics grades after controlling for prior GPA and course section. Most students reported using Khanmigo for homework help and exam prep, though lack of visuals and the Socratic design limited perceived usefulness for some students. Integrating genAI tutoring systems into class activities and setting student expectations may improve the likelihood of students using them effectively for learning.

items.title: Advanced Product and Systems Design Engineering in the Era of Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT)
items.abstract: The rapid convergence of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), distributed sensor networks, and edge-native artificial intelligence has transformed modern technology from isolated mechanical devices into complex, interconnected ecosystems. At the heart of this transformation lies Product and Systems Design Engineering (PSDE), a multidisciplinary discipline that bridges mechatronic engineering, human-centered design, software architecture, and systems engineering. This paper presents an extended theoretical and methodological framework for PSDE tailored specifically to Autonomous Robotics and the Internet of Things (IoT)—collectively conceptualized as the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT).We systematically examine the multi-layered lifecycle of IoRT development, addressing critical trade-offs between dynamic mechanical optimization, deterministic edge-computing, wireless network latency, cyber-physical security, and human-robot interaction (HRI). Furthermore, we detail the implementation of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation paradigms as mechanisms for risk mitigation and cost reduction. The paper concludes by outlining future design directions under the Industry 5.0 paradigm, highlighting the role of generative design, bio-inspired robotics, and circular lifecycle economics.

items.title: Advancing Patient‐Centred AI With Adaptive Machine Learning
items.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

items.abstract: An observational study of what a user does on the next turn after a ChatGPT-style assistant declines, using WildChat-1M. The dependent variable (press / follow the offered route / reframe / disengage) has real variance. The preregistered predictors mostly do not. This record includes a retraction. An exploratory contrast (capability limits produce fewer re-asks than policy refusals; 10/17 vs 11/42, Fisher p=.024) was found to be a coding collision: "press" had absorbed "walk the route the assistant offered." Re-coded, it is 6/17 vs 10/42, p=.52. Retracted 2026-10-22. Two preregistered tests failed: H1' is under-identified (predictors near-constant and co-occurring) and H2 is untestable (no frustration markers in 42 boundary turns). The boundary classification was independently validated on 84 turns by a second blind coder: kappa=.952. The dependent-variable coding was single-coder, which is the limitation that produced the error. Files: the preregistration text published before data collection (with its sha256), the full results document including codebook, reliability, re-code and limitations, and a deposit note stating the exact status of each claim. items.title: AgentDP: Towards Automated Model Deployment for Heterogeneous Embedded AI Applications
items.abstract: This paper presents AgentDP, which aims to deploy pre-trained AI models on heterogeneous embedded devices by fully automating model optimization and adaptation (O&A) with Large Language Model (LLM) agents. AgentDP not only significantly reduces human effort via automation but also enhances model inference efficacy by integrating LLMs with device-specific domain knowledge. To deliver a robust automation framework, AgentDP develops novel solutions to address three key technical challenges: 1) To help users elicit clear requirements, we propose a user requirement standardization module; 2) To mitigate the execution environment mismatch between AI models and heterogeneous embedded devices, we design an operator-aware model partition paradigm that enables different parts of the model to be efficiently executed on distinct inference engines. 3) To avoid re-searching optimization hyperparameters for new tasks, we propose a configuration reuse module that heuristically retrieves previous hyperparameter configurations for efficient reuse. Extensive experiments demonstrate that by fully automating the entire O&A process, AgentDP reduces entire model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual O&A while achieving higher task accuracy (more than 13% on average) than the baselines. Additionally, a comprehensive user study also exhibits the robust generalizability of AgentDP in adapting to different user requirements for heterogeneous embedded devices.

items.title: Agentic AI-Driven Digital Twin Frameworks for Predictive Toxicology and Autonomous Drug Safety Assessment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins, and computational pharmacology are changing the current approach to modern predictive toxicology and drug safety assessment. Traditional toxicity assessment tools are based on animal testing and non-dynamic computational models which are frequently limited in terms of scalability, and real-time toxicity forecasting. In this chapter, an agentic AI-based digital twin platform of predictive toxicology and autonomous drug safety evaluation is introduced. The suggested framework combines multimodal biomedical analytics, explainable AI (XAI), graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and federated learning to represent an intelligent ecosystem of toxicology. The system aids the adaptive simulation of toxicity, predicting toxicity individually, real-time pharmacological monitoring, and pharmacovigilance based on AI, enhances interpretability and privacy-preserving biomedical intelligence. Other significant applications, regulatory issues and future perspectives of next-generation intelligent drug safety systems are also discussed.

items.title: Agentic AI-Powered Expiry Date Management System
items.abstract: Food and medicines that pass their expiry dates cause avoidable financial loss, health risk and environmental harm, yet most expiry-tracking tools are passive reminder lists that depend on manual data entry. This paper proposes an Agentic AIPowered Expiry Date Management System in which a team of cooperating, tool-using AI agents autonomously captures product labels, extracts and validates expiry dates with optical character recognition (OCR), estimates shelf life when no date is printed, ranks items by spoilage risk, and acts on the result by sending timely alerts, suggesting recipes and routing surplus items to donation partners. A central orchestrator agent plans tasks, calls specialised agents and learns from user feedback, while a shared knowledge layer keeps inventory and food-safety rules consistent. We describe the architecture, the riskscoring model and the agent workflow, and report an illustrative simulation of 500 households over 60 days in which the agentic prioritisation policy reduced wasted items from 21.5% to 14.8% (c = 0.7) and 13.3% (c = 0.9). The modular design allows each agent to be upgraded or deployed independently in households, retail shelves and hospital pharmacies.

items.title: Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization
items.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.

items.title: AgenticEvolve: Evolutionary Program Search with Persistent Language Model Agents that Design and Run Experiments
items.abstract: Evolutionary program search with large language models keeps the structure of an evolutionary algorithm and uses the model as its variation operator. Typically, the model generates each candidate program in a single request from parent programs and their scores. We present AgenticEvolve, an evolutionary program search framework in which each island is run by a persistent large language model agent. Between evaluations, the agent designs and runs experiments on the candidate program. To measure the contribution of experimentation, we compare AgenticEvolve with No-analysis, an otherwise identical configuration with experiments disabled. On two heuristic design tasks with three large language models, AgenticEvolve produces better programs than No-analysis and OpenEvolve on both hidden and unseen instances. It reaches the baselines' final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground-truth structure of more equations than No-analysis and existing language-model and genetic programming baselines.

items.title: AgentPhishing: A Benchmark of LLM Email Agents Under Adaptive Attack
items.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.

items.title: AI Agent-Driven Datacenter Optimizer: A Guardrailed, Explainable LLM Orchestrator for Cloud Platform Management
items.abstract: Modern datacenters must balance three objectives that often conflict: keeping hardware within safe thermal limits, meeting latency expectations for high-priority work, and reducing the cost and carbon footprint of electricity. Traditional controllers handle these with fixed rules or heavily engineered optimization pipelines. This paper presents Grid Control, an autonomous datacenter orchestration system in which a large language model (LLM) acts as the decision-making agent. A simulated multi-region datacenter (5 regions, 15 servers, 60 chipsets) streams telemetry every second. Every decision interval the agent receives a frozen telemetry window and selects exactly one action from a small, closed vocabulary: shift_within_server, shift_within_region, migrate_region, or pass. A prioritized policy ranks overheating first, latency and load balance second, and cost and carbon third. Safety is enforced outside the model by a guardrail layer that routes high-criticality or administratorprohibited actions to a human approval queue. A feedback loop returns measured outcomes of past actions to the prompt as incontext learning signal, and a scope-restricted explainability module answers operator questions about the agent's behavior. Over 20 paired simulation runs, a deterministic stand-in for the agent's policy reduced time spent above the 68 °C threshold by about 24% and carbon-weighted load by about 9% relative to a no-agent baseline, with about 3% lower electricity cost. LLM-inthe-loop evaluation is left to future work. The contribution is an architecture and a reproducible testbed for studying safe, explainable, LLM-driven infrastructure control.

items.abstract: This systematic review investigated the medical potential of using artificial intelligence (AI) and holograms to improve body image as a means of maintaining sustainable and healthy beauty in the era of the longevity revolution. Although this review is a systematic review, it was conducted by individually setting related keywords according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) 2020 flowchart guidelines. The search method was as follows: PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus and IEEE Xplore were searched with the keywords “longevity revolution,” “artificial intelligence,” “Customized beauty device,” “Customized Cosmetics,”, “body image,” “hologram,” “hologram health,” “AI hologram,” and “healthy body image.” Accordingly, a total of 11,117 articles were searched. In the final stage, 56 articles were selected and included in the paper. The results of this study suggest that the world is moving towards the longevity revolution era due to the development of biotechnology, genetic engineering, and medicine, and that healthy beauty is needed in response to this. In addition, the development and use of AI and holograms in the medical field are continuing, suggesting the possibility of using them for obesity and body shape health management diet management. Therefore, this represents the AI domain of sustainable human security. It suggests the future necessity of developing personalized physical health management utilizing AI and holograms, as well as the infinite potential of customized beauty devices and cosmetics.

items.title: AI awareness and work stress among university teachers: The moderating roles of digital literacy and perceived organizational support
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) gradually enters the teaching and research contexts of higher education institutions, university teachers’ different perceptions of AI may elicit different psychological responses. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines the effects of AI Challenge Awareness and AI Threat Awareness on university teachers’ Work Stress, and further analyzes the moderating roles of Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support. Using university teachers as the research subjects, 421 valid samples were obtained through a questionnaire survey, and hierarchical regression analysis was employed to test the research hypotheses. The results indicate that AI Challenge Awareness is significantly and negatively correlated with university teachers’ Work Stress, whereas AI Threat Awareness is significantly and positively correlated with Work Stress. Both Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support significantly weaken the positive effect of AI Threat Awareness on Work Stress, but neither of their moderating effects on the relationship between AI Challenge Awareness and Work Stress reaches a significant level. The findings suggest that university teachers’ perceptions of AI do not merely manifest as a source of stress; rather, their effects depend on individuals’ different interpretations of the work-related changes brought about by AI. Compared with challenge-oriented perceptions, threat-oriented perceptions are more readily transformed into Work Stress, while Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support can, to a certain extent, buffer the stress induced by threat-oriented perceptions. The conclusions of this study help to deepen the understanding of individual differences in university teachers’ psychological responses in the context of AI, and provide references for higher education institutions to optimize the AI application environment and improve teacher support measures.

items.abstract: Abstract: Factchecking is among the key mechanisms for addressing information disorder. In the context of the growing integration of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, into the information environment, the need for reliable information is increasing while access to it is more challenging. Thus, generative artificial intelligence can be both – an asset and a risk to factcheckers. The present study aims to examine the extent to which Claude.ai and ChatGPT can factcheck claims in Bulgarian. The experiment was conducted using a free skill developed by Nauka.bg. The claims were selected from the “Verified” section of Factcheck.bg, the largest fact-checking platform in Bulgaria. Through comparative content analysis, the study found that in most cases both models correctly identify false claims in accordance with Factcheck.bg’s publications. Claude.ai demonstrates a more authoritative tone and provides concise explanations supporting its verdicts. ChatGPT is more hesitant but offers greater detail, precision, and clarity in its explanations. Notably, ChatGPT rarely references its sources, whereas Claude.ai occasionally links to unreliable sources. A positive trend is Claude.ai’s note to consult official factchecking organizations and verified information sources.The results confirm the hypothesis that artificial intelligence can assist factcheckers but cannot replace human expertise in the verification process. items.abstract: Scientific research usually begins with a question, followed by a review of existing work, the development of possible The reasons for this, the planning of the experiments or simulations, and a careful verification of the results. Now artificial intelligence (AI) is being used can be used to help with a number of these steps. items.title: AI Governance and the Architecture of Dependency
items.abstract: A system does not have to remove choice in order to shape it. It can define the problem, structure the options that appear, and create conditions under which a voluntary choice becomes costly to reverse. These mechanisms predate artificial intelligence. This paper asks what changes when AI-mediated systems operate them at greater speed, scale, and adaptability, and when the people subject to them cannot practically inspect, contest, or leave. The paper develops a four-part lens (problem definition, choice architecture, dependency formation, reversibility) and distinguishes institutional dependency from epistemic dependency. It adds an agency and accountability audit of six questions: who sets the objective, who controls the data, model and infrastructure, who can inspect the evidence, who bears the cost of error, who can override or replace the system, and what alternatives remain. Its central hypothesis, an accountability asymmetry, is stated with the evidence that would weaken it. A rubric scores safeguards by whether they have been exercised, not merely documented, and is applied to three current arrangements: the Robodebt scheme, the Medicare WISeR model, and the UnitedHealth nH Predict litigation. Where public evidence allows no score, the gap is reported as a finding. Appendices provide a one-page citizen audit card and a legal and case status snapshot as of 21 October 2026. This is a working paper. It has not been peer reviewed and is not legal advice. Claims are labelled documented, reported, interpretation, or hypothesis. The rubric is unvalidated and was scored by a single rater from public sources. Companion to Johnson (2026a) and Johnson (2026b).

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming drug discovery and pharmacology by enabling data-driven, predictive, and system-level approaches across the drug development lifecycle. Overall, it presents a forward-looking roadmap for responsible, regulatory-grade AI adoption in pharmacological research and drug development.

items.title: AI literacy is directly associated with positive attitudes and indirectly associated with negative attitudes through AI anxiety: a cross-sectional study of preservice teachers
items.abstract: Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

items.title: AI PCs and On-Device Artificial Intelligence: The Future of Intelligent Computing
items.abstract: AI PCs and on-device artificial intelligence are changing how everyday computers use AI. Instead of sending every request to a remote cloud server, a device can process suitable tasks locally using its CPU, GPU, and specialised neural processing unit (NPU). This can reduce response time, limit data transfer, support some functions without a stable internet connection, and give users more control over personal data. The practical value of these benefits depends on the task, the model, and the computer's hardware. Local processing also has to work within limits such as memory capacity, power consumption, heat, and model size. This review discusses three research works: a comprehensive survey of on-device AI models, a study proposing a collaborative consumer edge-AI ecosystem, and research on on-device AI for smart environments and Industry 4.0. The papers are compared by focus, approach, contribution, and limitation. The review identifies model optimisation, efficient hardware use, privacy-aware collaboration, and energy management as important areas. It also finds that the selected works do not establish a common benchmark specifically for AI PCs. A task-aware local/cloud architecture is proposed for future study; it has not been experimentally tested.

items.title: AI Service Investment and Information Disclosure Under Financing Strategies in a Tourism Live-Streaming Supply Chain: The Roles of Government Regulation and Platform Altruism
items.abstract: Live-streaming plays a vital role in tourism product marketing. Consumers often struggle to obtain sufficient product information through live-streaming, leading to information asymmetry and low trust, which hinder transaction efficiency. To address these challenges, an increasing number of live-streaming platforms are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) services to help consumers better understand tourism products. However, investment in AI services requires substantial financial resources, while suppliers’ information disclosure directly affects the transparency of tourism product information. A Stackelberg game model examines how government regulation and financing strategies shape supplier information disclosure, platform AI investment, and supply chain profits. The results show the following: (1) The platform’s financing choice is not determined solely by financing costs. The relative advantage of supplier financing over bank financing depends jointly on relative financing rates, consumers’ sensitivity to AI services, and the platform’s altruistic preference; (2) Neither strategy dominates. Subsidies are more advantageous when reward-and-penalty intensity is low, whereas reward-and-penalty regulation becomes preferable as the intensity increases. (3) Platform altruism boosts AI investment and supplier profit but may reduce platform profit when commissions are low or consumers are less AI-sensitive. These findings provide theoretical guidance for live-streaming platforms to optimize their financing and AI service investment decisions, and for governments to design differentiated information disclosure regulations.

items.title: AI source disclosure in sustainable advertising: felt obligation, competence framing and decision-making orientation
items.abstract: Purpose This research examines when and why artificial intelligence (AI) source disclosure reduces participation in sustainable advertising. It proposes that AI source disclosure is associated with lower felt obligation toward the campaign organization and that this negative effect depends on appeal type and decision-making orientation. Design/methodology/approach Five experiments tested the proposed model. Study 1 used an interactive webpage and a consequential sharing task to examine actual participation. Study 2 examined felt obligation as the proposed mediator while testing perceived sincerity as an alternative explanation. Studies 3 and 4 tested the moderating role of warmth versus competence appeals in Chinese and US samples, respectively. Study 5 examined instrumental versus normative decision-making as an additional boundary condition. Findings Campaigns attributed to AI sources generated lower participation than campaigns attributed to human sources. This effect was associated with reduced felt obligation toward the organization, while sincerity and authenticity were not supported as mediators. The negative effect was stronger for warmth appeals and normative decision-making, but weaker for competence appeals and instrumental decision-making. Originality/value This research identifies felt obligation toward the campaign organization as a pathway associated with responses to AI source disclosure in sustainable advertising. It extends the stereotype content model by demonstrating that appeal type conditions the AI source-disclosure effect and contributes to stakeholder and AI decision-making research by identifying decision-making orientation as an additional boundary condition.

items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated into business training and development (T&D) to strengthen organizational capacity for long-term viability. items.title: AI-Based Air Quality Monitoring and Pollution Control
items.abstract: Air pollution is a major environmental concern because it affects human health, ecosystems, and the quality of life in urban and industrial areas. Traditional monitoring systems often depend on fixed stations and manual sampling. Although these methods provide useful measurements, they may have high operating costs, limited spatial coverage, and delays in reporting. Recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), and wireless sensors offer ways to monitor air quality continuously and forecast pollution levels. This review examines four supplied papers covering AI and ML models with wireless sensors, IoT-based monitoring, comparisons between traditional and AI-based methods, and a proposed smart-city forecasting framework. The reviewed literature describes applications such as missing-data estimation, sensor calibration, anomaly detection, Air Quality Index (AQI) estimation, and short-term pollution forecasting. Models including regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, neural networks, and deep-learning methods are discussed. The papers also identify challenges related to data quality, sensor reliability, cost, scalability, model transfer between locations, and system integration. One proposed framework reports improved prediction results, but these figures are treated as results reported by that paper rather than independently verified findings. Overall, AI can support earlier warnings and better-informed pollution management when it is combined with reliable sensors , quality data, and local validation.

items.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive review of the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin (DT) technologies in advanced predictive maintenance (PdM) in modern industrial ecosystems. items.title: AI-Based PDF Chat and Summarization Engine Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Portable Document Format (PDF) files are the most common way of storing reports, research papers, manuals, and legal documents, but their layout-oriented structure makes them difficult to search and to query conversationally. Large Language Models (LLMs) can answer questions fluently, but they may hallucinate and cannot process long documents that exceed a fixed context window. This study presents the design, implementation, and preliminary testing of a PDF chat and summarization system based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system uses a three-stage data pipeline (raw, processed, and RAG-ready) that parses PDFs, removes repeating headers and footers, converts content to Markdown, and applies structure-aware chunking, which attaches section-path metadata to every chunk. Answers are generated by the openai/gpt-oss-120b model (served through the Groq API) using passages retrieved from a local ChromaDB vector store with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings, and are returned with page references. Three chunking strategies (fixed-size, Markdown-aware, and hierarchical) are defined, and an evaluation protocol based on answer accuracy, faithfulness, hit rate at k, unsupported-answer rate, and response time is specified for comparing them. In preliminary testing, the system processed uploaded PDFs and answered natural-language questions with an average response time of approximately 2–5 seconds. A full comparative evaluation is left for future work. The study provides a reproducible, small-scale baseline that student and small-team developers can extend, and it argues that document preprocessing and chunking quality are central to the reliability of PDF question answering

items.title: AI-Based Plagiarism Checker: A Review of Text Similarity, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and AI-Obfuscated Plagiarism Detection
items.abstract: Digital documents, paraphrasing tools and large language models have made plagiarism much harder to catch than plain copy-and-paste matching. This review looks at five research papers that approach academic plagiarism detection from different directions: a systematic literature survey, text-based feature selection, deep learning, a comparison of detection techniques, and the detection of AI-obfuscated plagiarism in modeling assignments. Between them, the studies draw on lexical overlap, sentence structure, semantic similarity, writing style and token sequences taken from structured modeling artifacts. One study pairs Chi-square feature selection with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) and reports F-measure scores of 89.34% on PAN 2013 and 92.95% on PAN 2014; another reports that its LSTM-based system placed first among the systems it was compared with on the same benchmarks. A more recent approach for modeling assignments normalizes tokens, matches them automatically and leaves the final judgement to a human inspector, which makes it more resistant to AI-based obfuscation. Taken together, the papers show that no single similarity measure can handle every kind of plagiarism. A practical AI-based checker should therefore combine fast candidate retrieval, several text and structure features, carefully validated machine-learning models and human review. Open problems include resistance to paraphrasing, coverage of datasets and languages, fair evaluation, and the danger of reading a detector score as conclusive proof.

items.title: AI-Based Smart Cow Shelter Analysis and Management System Using Internet of Things and Machine Learning
items.abstract: Cow shelters need coordination between animal identification, health observations, activity tracking, environmental factors, feed and water supplies, vaccination schedules, medical records, and operational actions. Precision livestock farming has created useful tools using sensors, identification systems and artificial intelligence. Recent reviews still show problems with combining information, checking data quality, making systems work together, and supporting decisions [1] [2] [7] [10] [24]. This paper introduces a cow-shelter system that connects RFID animal tagging, different types of IoT sensors, ESP32-based data collection at the edge, Wi-Fi communication, Flask web services, MySQL databases, clear rule-based alerts, and machine learning—all within a single management process. The system links animal data with shelter-zone details and keeps track of time, data quality, management actions, and past alerts. The analysis is done in stages: simple rules give alerts, and machine learning comes later once enough labelled and checked data is available. Features used in the analysis include sensor readings, changes over time, average trends, activity summaries, environmental data, and feed and water status. A repeatable way to test the system is created, measuring sensing delay, alert timing, data transmission reliability, dashboard speed, recovery after failure, and how well predictions work. The main contribution is not in technology but in the full system design: an information-to-action process built around animal identity, multiple sensors, resource tracking, records, analysis, alerts, and human input. The paper does not give accuracy or timing results and does not claim the individual parts are new.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Sustainable Fisheries Management and Intelligent Aquatic Water Resource Monitoring
items.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly proposed as a means of linking aquatic observations, predictive models and management decisions. Their relevance to sustainability nevertheless depends on more than the speed or accuracy of an artificial intelligence model. This critical narrative review examines the evidence connecting digital-twin architectures with capture fisheries, aquaculture and freshwater and coastal water-quality monitoring. Literature published through 30 July 2026 was selected through targeted scholarly searches, citation tracing and bibliographic verification, with particular attention to observation quality, independent validation, operational feedback and management outcomes. The synthesis distinguishes a digital model, a continuously updated digital representation and a decision-linked twin, and separates component performance from demonstrated ecological benefit. Evidence supports advances in image-based monitoring, satellite retrievals, hybrid environmental prediction and selected field deployments. It is substantially less conclusive regarding sustained stock recovery, equitable allocation or ecosystem-scale benefits attributable to a complete digital-twin system. Important limitations include imperfect observability, inappropriate spatial and temporal validation, uncertain transfer between environments, simulator-dependent policy optimisation and incomplete treatment of human behaviour. Apparent disagreement between promising technical demonstrations and limited management evidence largely reflects different endpoints and system boundaries rather than a simple conflict over technological feasibility. A federated, decision-centred framework is proposed in which traceable observations support uncertainty-aware state estimation, explicit management objectives, constrained decision support and independently audited outcomes. The framework includes staged deployment, human authorisation, local data governance and lifecycle assessment; it is an unvalidated synthesis rather than an implemented system. Near-term priorities are prospective forecasting benchmarks, comparative management trials, failure-tolerant monitoring and participatory evaluation in data-limited fisheries. Digital twins are most defensible as accountable extensions of existing environmental observation and adaptive management, not as substitutes for ecological understanding, enforceable institutions or legitimate collective decisions.

items.title: AI-Driven Economic Transformation and Employment Dynamics in India 2047: Opportunities, Challenges, and Policy Pathways toward Viksit Bharat
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a nascent technology that could become a general-purpose technology and can have significant impacts on economic development, productivity growth, labour markets and good governance. The study will delve into the potential impact of Artificial Intelligence on the economy and job landscape of India as part of the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. The study uses qualitative review-based research methodology that is based on analyzing evidence from the academic literature, government documents, as well as reports produced by national and international institutions. AI has the potential to augment productivity, innovate solutions, modernize industries, contribute to digital governance and create job opportunities, as revealed by this study. At the same time, the implementation of AI can be challenging due to the changes in labor markets, lack of skills, digital divide, fragility of the informal sector, data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic biases, and institutional preparedness. In this study, it is argued that AI will not necessarily take the place of jobs, but rather change the employment type if suitable reskilling measures are taken. It identifies the following policy priorities – human capital, digital infrastructure, responsible AI governance, research and innovation, and social protection.

items.title: AI-Driven Project Management Automation: A Framework for Task Prioritization, Progress Monitoring, and Risk Identification
items.abstract: Project management requires coordination of tasks, deadlines, dependencies, resources, and risks. Manual status reporting and inconsistent prioritisation can make emerging delivery problems difficult to identify. This paper proposes and demonstrates a framework connecting task prioritisation, progress monitoring, and task-delay risk identification. The framework combines transparent rule-based scoring, monitoring flags, a machine-learning classifier, and human review. A prototype was evaluated using 1,000 generated task records, with a Decision Tree compared against a majority-class baseline on a held-out test set. The Decision Tree achieved 61.0% accuracy, 27.4% precision, 57.5% recall, and an F1-score of 37.1% for the delay class. The baseline achieved 80.0% accuracy but detected no delayed tasks, demonstrating why accuracy alone can be misleading in imbalanced classification. These results describe the prototype experiment and do not establish effectiveness on real project records. The paper concludes that an integrated framework can provide a reproducible basis for further evaluation, with real-world validation required before operational use. Keywords: artificial intelligence, project management automation, task prioritisation, progress monitoring, risk identification, delay prediction, Decision Tree, business analytics

items.title: AI-Driven Sustainability Education in Business Schools: Expectations of Educators
items.abstract: Accelerated progress in digital technologies has influenced all industries. Interest in embracing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education and research is flourishing among scholars, practitioners, educators, students, and the general public. Educational institutions now need to transform their traditional approach towards teaching and research by implementing innovative technologies. However, controversies surrounding the use of AI in education or research require deeper examination. Moreover, integration sustainability in business education has become an obligation for universities around the world. The significance of universities in empowering generations to tackle complex sustainability issues calls for ground-breaking solutions. In this regard, AI with its immense capabilities can offer a unique approach. This chapter aims to explore AI trends and tendencies in teaching and research and to shed light on the role of AI in sustainability education. The main research question is: How can AI be incorporated into teaching to enhance sustainability education? To achieve research aims, the qualitative research method was used and expert interview approach was applied. This research contributes to the discussion of introducing AI in sustainability education and research agenda by delving into the multifaceted intersection of AI, sustainability and education. Based on the results, a theoretical framework is proposed to adopt AI into sustainable development teaching. The findings benefit academics, educators, researchers, policymakers and industry representatives to grasp future trends in sustainability education through AI-powered initiatives.

items.title: AI-Enabled Decision Support for Volunteer Allocation in Disaster Management: A Three-Stage Optimization Framework
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming disaster management through intelligent decision support, predictive resource allocation, and adaptive operational planning. Volunteer management — a critical yet underexplored challenge in humanitarian logistics — represents a domain where AI-driven optimization can deliver substantial operational gains. This chapter presents a three-stage AI-enabled decision support framework for volunteer allocation in large-scale disaster response. At its core is a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that constitutes the optimization layer of a broader AI-assisted humanitarian logistics ecosystem. The model assigns volunteers to disaster management centers while maximizing demand satisfaction, respecting capacity and travel-time constraints, incorporating individual preferences, enforcing group cohesion to improve long-term retention, and preventing scheduling conflicts. Computational experiments using a synthetic scenario with 100 volunteers, six volunteer types, four disaster management centers, and a seven-day response horizon confirm the model’s feasibility: the MILP solver reaches a solution in under 8 seconds and generates schedules that substantially reduce unmet demand. Sensitivity analysis on the preference–demand trade-off reveals important operational dynamics. The chapter concludes with a roadmap for extending the framework with machine learning demand forecasting, reinforcement learning-based dynamic reassignment, digital twin simulation, and predictive retention modeling — positioning the system as a foundation for next-generation AI tools in disaster humanitarian logistics.

items.title: AI-Enabled School Management for Sustainable Education: A Systematic Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: This review examines the various ways artificial intelligence (AI) can influence school management and its potential to promote sustainable education. It brings together the findings from earlier studies to illustrate how schools are using AI to simplify administrative tasks, enrich learning experiences, and support sustainable education efforts. Key uses include AI tools for real-time data analysis, better resource management, and personalised learning paths that connect students with real-world environmental issues. By managing tasks such as data cleaning and report generation, AI enables educators and staff to dedicate more time to strategic initiatives like developing curricula and engaging the community in sustainability projects. The review also highlights major challenges and risks of using AI in education, such as concerns about data privacy, the need for reliable infrastructure, and ethical issues related to algorithmic bias. The findings show that although AI provides powerful tools for creating efficient and environmentally conscious schools, successful and fair implementation requires careful planning, targeted teacher training, and a focus on equal access. The article concludes by emphasising key areas for future research, underlining the need for robust frameworks to enable schools to use AI responsibly while promoting both academic excellence and a culture of sustainability and sustainable education.
