items.title: AI-generated content-plagiarism versus institutional silence: comparative insights on responses of higher education to rapid technological changes in China and Japan
items.abstract: This study seeks to elucidate how the higher education systems of China and Japan have addressed the issue of plagiarism exacerbated by generative artificial intelligence (AIGC-plagiarism) and the insights gained from these responses. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated with higher education, the age-old problem of plagiarism has resurfaced with greater intensity and elusiveness, sweeping across universities worldwide. Although no definitive consensus exists regarding the precise definition of AIGC-plagiarism, this conceptual ambiguity does not preclude its broad recognition as prohibited academic conduct. The relationship between cutting-edge technologies and higher education appears to have reached an impasse, yet the majority of Chinese institutions have maintained a stance of silence, while the Chinese government has shown concern but refrained from taking formal action. This research comparatively examines the response strategies to AIGC-plagiarism by the Japanese government and 359 universities, which share similar systemic and institutional contexts with their Chinese counterparts, and reaches a conclusion that the practice of “No Copy + Exceptions” emerges as a particularly instructive approach. A micro-level comparative analysis reveals that this regulatory inertia is shaped by both technological and political factors, and represents a pragmatic strategy in the face of technological uncertainty. Regardless of the underlying rationale, such silence constitutes an unacceptable form of de facto endorsement or passive acquiescence. Higher education systems must develop more proactive, responsive, and agile mechanisms to cultivate morally anchored, innovation-capable students amidst technological and geopolitical turbulence. Key components of this mechanism include, but are not limited to a unified national benchmark and implementation rule, a dynamic AI impact assessment structure, autonomy of faculty and academic councils, and student participation with feedback channels.

items.title: AI-Guided Reflection to Bridge Formal Learning and Work
items.abstract: Formal on-demand online courses offer professionals a structured way to acquire knowledge that is relevant to their work, and can complement workplace learning. However, connecting between such formal learning and work brings two essential challenges: (1) identifying and articulating work-grounded learning objectives and mapping them to formal learning; and (2) transferring knowledge newly acquired in the learning space to the workplace. Reflection, guided by AI tools, may be a useful way to support these processes. This chapter first frames reflective practice as a way of working—with continuous reflection alongside work—and then presents three cases where AI-guided reflection bridged formal learning and work. In a socio-technical design space, AI tools can prompt and structure reflection, provide feedback, and offer data analytics as a “looking glass” on work practice. In doing so, they steer attention and shape how professionals reflect. At the same time, professionals retain agency to choose, configure, and use tools; but professionals’ competence is a pre-requisite for effective such reflective practice. Subsequently, our vision for technology-oriented research is to further develop systems that (1) facilitate the articulation of learning needs, (2) facilitate knowledge transfer by using rich and multimodal evidence from the workplace to support AI-guided reflection, and (3) expand interaction affordances towards more situated and embodied AI-guidance (e.g., multimodal sensing and analytics, ambient prompts, voice-first coaching, agentic companions) that may better fit workplace constraints and ways of working, and (4) help professionals further develop their agency in reflective practice through such hybrid, multimodal and embodied AI. In parallel, a challenge for workplace learning-oriented research is to examine AI-guidance in-situ and to develop socio-technical AI design patterns, as combinations of technology design and usage. Formal on-demand learning providers are uniquely positioned to take up such AI-guidance as part of their offerings, with a recommendation to provide both tools and training in using tools, and teaching, coaching, and mentoring to build professionals’ reflection competence.

items.abstract: Ethical, scientific and translational limitations of animal testing have increased the global pursuit of high quality, human relevant, biomedical research, toxicological, and drug development alternatives. The combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and cell-based assays, organ-on-chip (OoC) technologies, and computational modelling, is transforming the paradigm of experimental research by promoting predictive, scalable, and ethically responsible research. items.title: AI-Powered Nano-Drones for Pest Detection, Crop Monitoring, and Waste Valorization
items.abstract: This chapter analyzes how artificial intelligence (AI) and nano-drones can be used as a revolutionary method to make agriculture sustainable. It presents new AI-drone architects that can target two fundamental uses: the precision control of pests and automated waste valorization. We show how high-resolution optical and multispectral sensors on AI-enabled nano-drones can provide an early warning of pests and eco-friendly pesticide control by reducing chemical use. We discuss the contribution of an AI-based waste valorization system in which nano-drones automatically detect, classify, and harvest farm waste to be converted into bioenergy and organic fertilizers. A machine-learning algorithm allows these drones to predict waste types and optimize downstream processes. The chapter also outlines real-time monitoring of crops using drone sensors to measure health levels of plants, soil nutrients, and irrigation requirements to provide predictive analytics to optimize crop yields. Critical issues such as regulatory frameworks, data privacy, and infrastructure shortcomings, which need to be overcome for deployment at scale, are discussed. The chapter provides a data-driven, automation-focused framework to AI-enabled nano-drones in sustainable agriculture.

items.title: Airway image analysis systems: a review of datasets, evaluation methodologies, and deep learning approaches
items.abstract: Airway image analysis systems play an increasingly important role in computer-assisted diagnosis, quantitative airway assessment, intervention planning, and respiratory disease management. However, the development of robust airway analysis methods remains challenging due to the complex geometry of airway structures, strong class imbalance, variability in imaging protocols, and the need to preserve anatomical connectivity across multiple spatial scales. Recent advances in topology-aware learning, transformer-based architectures, and foundation-model adaptation have substantially changed the landscape of airway image analysis, motivating an updated review focused specifically on airway-oriented systems. In this narrative review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the datasets, evaluation methodologies, and computational approaches that underpin modern airway image analysis systems. We discuss the imaging modalities and publicly available datasets commonly used for airway analysis and examine their strengths, limitations, and implications for algorithm development and benchmarking. Particular attention is given to evaluation methodologies, including overlap-based, surface-distance, and topology-aware metrics that assess both segmentation accuracy and structural correctness. We further review the evolution of computational approaches, covering convolutional neural networks, transformer-based architectures, hybrid methods, topology-aware and tubular-aware networks, foundation-model adaptations, and data-efficient learning strategies. Finally, we discuss current challenges related to dataset availability, annotation quality, model generalization, topology preservation, and clinical deployment, and outline future research directions toward robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable airway image analysis systems.

items.title: Algebraic Structures for Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Decision-Making Systems
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important research direction because intelligent systems are increasingly used to support decisions in complex and uncertain environments. However, the interpretability of a decision depends not only on the final prediction but also on the mathematical structure through which the prediction is obtained. This paper develops an algebraic framework for interpretable multi-criteria decision-making based on bounded ordered structures, weighted aggregation, and explicit criterion-level contributions. A finite set of alternatives is evaluated using normalized criteria, and a weighted score is assigned to each alternative. The framework represents criterion values in a bounded lattice and uses an order-preserving aggregation operator to obtain transparent rankings. Mathematical properties concerning monotonicity, boundedness, score decomposition, and stability under perturbations are established. An illustrative numerical example involving the selection of an artificial intelligence model demonstrates how the framework generates rankings and human-readable explanations. The approach provides a mathematically explicit foundation for decision support and can be extended to fuzzy, linguistic, and neutrosophic environments. The proposed framework and numerical example are illustrative; novelty and performance claims require literature verification and empirical validation. Keywords: Abstract algebra; lattice theory; explainable artificial intelligence; multi-criteria decision-making; interpretable decision systems; weighted aggregation.

items.title: Algorithmic Childhood Future-AI Prediction Systems and the Pre-Emption of Choice in Young Consumers
items.abstract: The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.

items.title: Algorithmic drift in generative adaptive learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence promises to democratize personalized tutoring, yet the longitudinal stability of adaptive systems remains under-theorized. Current ethical discourse focuses on static bias. This paper argues that a distinct threat lies in algorithmic drift: a feedback loop in which minor, demographically asymmetric observation errors compound over time into systemic inequities. We make three contributions. First, we formalize algorithmic drift as a coupled learner--tutor dynamical system. Second, we corroborate this theory with an agent-based Monte Carlo simulation in which either a transparent online tracker or an LSTM deep-knowledge-tracing network drives an IRT-based curriculum policy. Third, we introduce the temporal fairness stabilizer (TFS), a targeted intervention that periodically re-probes learner capability, and benchmark it against standard exploration baselines with explicit group-fairness metrics and replication-level inference. Within the modeled environment, TFS closes the achievement gap where generic exploration does not, and we characterize the conditions under which it succeeds. We separate what is established analytically, what is demonstrated in simulation, and what remains to be validated with real learners. Our results reframe algorithmic fairness in education as a temporal property of a closed loop rather than a deployment-time checkbox.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC WILDERNESS: AI LITERACY, TECHNOLOGICAL MEDIATION, AND DECISION-MAKING AMONG GENERATION Z HIKERS
items.abstract: This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of Thai Generation Z hikers, thoroughly examining the critical intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and complex decision-making in wilderness environments. As young adventurers increasingly pursue nature-based eco-experientia for psychological restoration, AI has rapidly evolved into an active, front-facing backcountry companion. Using the Theory of Technological Mediation alongside robust methodological triangulation—including in-depth interviews, focus groups, and interactive discussions with university-aged hikers—this research examines how algorithmic tools profoundly reshape human-nature relationships. The empirical findings clearly show that AI is seamlessly integrated throughout the trekking lifecycle, functioning as a vital digital safety net that mitigates environmental uncertainty. However, this deep integration precipitates a highly complex socio-technical paradox. While participants consistently exhibit exceptional functional AI literacy, an emerging algorithmic dependency actively threatens to erode traditional, intuitive wilderness judgment. Ultimately, AI facilitates a hermeneutic relationship in which pristine nature is interpreted through curated data, fundamentally transforming raw exploration into a mediated digital reality that urgently requires careful preservation of human agency within adventure tourism.

items.title: An adaptable methodology for generating realistic annotated synthetic data with 3D Gaussian splatting and modeling software
items.abstract: The increasing demand for large annotated datasets in computer vision underscores the need for scalable synthetic data generation methods, as traditional approaches often lack adaptability or offer limited annotations. To address these challenges, this work introduces a comprehensive methodology that leverages 3D Gaussian splatting and Blender to generate photorealistic synthetic datasets with automatic annotations, suitable for training deep learning computer vision models in multiple tasks, including object detection, pose estimation, semantic and instance segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal estimation. Designed for broad applicability, this approach was developed with the significant challenges of industrial scenarios in mind, where data scarcity impedes the development of resilient AI-based situational awareness systems. The proposed pipeline can model any target scenario by reconstructing high-fidelity 3D environments, integrating synthetic objects through diverse modeling techniques, and applying procedural generation to vary lighting, camera angles, and object placements. With all annotations generated automatically, this approach facilitates the efficient creation of extensive annotated datasets, thereby eliminating manual labeling efforts. To validate the effectiveness of our synthetic data, we train computer vision models exclusively on these datasets and evaluate their performance in real applications, demonstrating their generalization capability and practical relevance. The results confirm that our methodology provides a scalable, flexible, and high-quality alternative to traditional data collection, bridging the gap between synthetic and real-world datasets while offering a powerful tool for both research and industrial applications. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/juanjesus-ldo/scene_generator .

items.title: An Empirical Study of Recent Large Language Models for Knowledge Graph to Text Generation on Standard Benchmarks
items.abstract: Knowledge graph-to-text (KG-to-text) generation verbalizes a set of knowledge graph triples into fluent natural language. While fine-tuned encoder-decoder models have long been the standard approach, recent LLMs are becoming increasingly competitive. We benchmark recent LLMs against fine-tuned encoder-decoder models, using reference-based metrics and graph-grounded reference-free LLM-based evaluation validated against human annotations. We observed that recent LLMs substantially narrow, and in several settings close, the gap with fine-tuned models on reference-based metrics, while performing better on graph-grounded metrics. LLM-based evaluation scores show limited correlation with reference-based metrics, suggesting that the two approaches capture different aspects of generation quality. Graph-grounded evaluation reveals that prompted models produce fewer contradictions and triple omissions than fine-tuned models, and these errors increase more rapidly with graph size for fine-tuned models, highlighting differences between the two approaches that reference-based metrics may not fully capture.

items.title: An evidence-informed operational blueprint for delivering focused clinical daily safety huddles in clinical practice
items.abstract: Despite sustained attention to patient safety, avoidable harm remains prevalent in acute and rehabilitation settings, often arising from communication failures, fragmented teamwork and limited situational awareness. Traditional safety mechanisms are largely reactive and do not consistently support real-time risk management. Focused clinical daily safety huddles (FCDSHs) have emerged as a proactive, nurse-led intervention to close this gap. FCDSHs are structured, multidisciplinary and action oriented, with a focus on identifying and mitigating avoidable patient safety risks. Effective implementation requires preparation, consistent facilitation, multidisciplinary engagement and psychological safety, supported by proportionate documentation and clear escalation processes. Nursing leadership is central to embedding and sustaining FCDSHs within routine clinical practice. Making FCDSHs part of routine care strengthens situational awareness and teamwork while proactively mitigating avoidable patient safety risks.

items.title: An investigation of lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, and work-related outcomes among female teachers: mixed-methods evidence for occupational health promotion
items.abstract: Background Teachers’ health and quality of life are important to school health and education policy. This study examined lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, satisfaction, and health-related absence among female schoolteachers in Saudi Arabia. Methods A mixed-methods study in the Eastern Province combined a cross-sectional questionnaire completed by 562 female government-school teachers with semi-structured interviews with 19 teachers. Mental well-being was assessed using the WHO-5. Associations were examined using Spearman correlation and multivariable logistic regression. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive approach. Results Poor mental well-being (WHO-5 ≤ 50) was reported by 58.4% of teachers, and 24.4% scored ≤28. No moderate-intensity activity was reported by 42.3%; 77.4% of 561 respondents slept six hours or less. Unhealthy foods were consumed several times per week or almost daily by 52.5%; only 29.9% consumed fruit and vegetables daily. Poor or very poor sleep quality was reported by 19.4%, and tobacco use by 3.4%. Overall, 27.9% brushed their teeth less than twice daily, and 52.1% last visited a dentist over two years earlier. Tooth or gum pain at least sometimes during the preceding three months was reported by 61.9%. Sleep quality and duration showed moderate positive correlations with well-being ( r = 0.390 and 0.302, respectively; p < 0.001). Physical activity, dietary behaviors, toothbrushing, and oral pain were also associated with well-being. Higher teaching load was weakly associated with lower satisfaction ( r = −0.098, p = 0.020). Lifestyle and satisfaction scores remained associated with good well-being after adjustment (OR = 1.051, 95% CI: 1.030–1.073; and 1.035, 95% CI: 1.022–1.048, respectively). Self-rated health also remained associated with good well-being. Lower lifestyle and well-being scores were associated with more health-related absence (all p < 0.05). Five themes described demanding workdays, barriers to healthy routines, emotional strain, work extending into home life, and occupational health concerns. Conclusion Unhealthy daily routines and poor mental well-being were common among teachers. These findings support greater attention to teacher health in education policy. School health promotion should include manageable work demands, time for rest, and access to preventive care. Sustained investment in workplace health promotion may support teachers’ well-being and quality of life.

items.title: An LLM-based decision aid for collaborative decision-making in juvenile idiopathic arthritis: A multimethod evaluation
items.abstract: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common pediatric chronic inflammatory rheumatic condition, with substantial quality-of-life impacts. Treatment selection is complex due to limited guideline evidence, and difficult trade-offs. Decisions are often solely physician driven. We evaluated the feasibility of Large Language Model-based Decision Aid (LLM-DA) designed to support collaborative rather than solely physician decision-making in JIA care. A multi-method feasibility study was conducted in accordance with the TRIPOD-LLM checklist. The aims were twofold: first, to assess the quality of the LLM-DA (OpenAI’s o3 model) based on evaluations from three pediatric rheumatologists and an exploratory assessment by an LLM-as-a-Judge (OpenAI’s GPT-5 model); and second, to characterize perceived value of the tool from the patient perspective through a mixed methods evaluation (n = 34). For 10 de-identified use cases, rheumatologists and LLM-Judge generated treatment recommendations and scored the LLM-DA outputs on safety, factual consistency, treatment appropriateness, and preference acknowledgment. Rheumatologists rated 97% of outputs as acceptable for safety and preference acknowledgment, 60% for factual consistency, 70% for appropriateness. Treatment recommendation agreement among all evaluators and real-world data was low at <30%. Inter-rater agreement for scores among rheumatologists was almost perfect for safety and preference acknowledgement, moderate for treatment appropriateness, and poor for factual consistency, and remained the same or improved with LLM-as-a-Judge. Variability in evaluator scoring and treatment recommendations may reflect the inherent heterogeneity in acceptable JIA treatment pathways and potential limitations in the LLM-DA’s decision-making logic. Five patient themes were identified: the tool complements rheumatologist expertise, prepares patients through reflection and actionable information, builds confidence for self-advocacy, has variable value depending on the patient-physician relationship, and has potential for broader JIA self-management. items.title: An Old Answer to a New Problem: The Degree-Free Model for Higher Education in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Generative AI has not created the governance crisis in higher education credentialing; it has made it harder to ignore. The academic degree is higher education’s principal instrument for governing access to occupations. Its signaling value depends on assessed work reflecting individual competence. AI weakens that link: in blind marking, AI-written exam answers went largely undetected and, on average, outscored students, while detection tools trail each new model. Strengthening surveillance restores procedural control only at the cost of assessment validity. Drawing on credentialism and signaling theory, this paper argues that the response may need to include institutional redesign, not only pedagogical adjustment. It proposes a degree-free model, illustrated by the yeshiva: a centuries-old institution organized around formation, community, and recognized mastery rather than certification. Labor markets already partly follow this logic, as employers substitute direct observation of performance for the degree within three to five years of hire. Three recommendations follow. Outside safety-critical fields, institutions could stop issuing degrees while continuing to teach. Public investment should shift from surveillance-based assessment toward authentic evaluation. Reform should be differentiated by field, retaining mandatory credentialing in licensed and safety-critical professions. The model is offered as a proposition for debate, not a blueprint.

items.title: Analysis of Big Data-Based Financial Technology and AI on Financial Inclusion in Indonesia
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of implementing Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based financial technology on increasing financial inclusion in Indonesia during the period 2019–2024. The background of this study is based on the rapid increase in digital transformation in the financial sector triggered by the adoption of fintech, but there is still a gap in financial access, especially among low-income groups and disadvantaged regions. This study uses a quantitative approach with a panel data model, involving independent variables of Gross Regional Domestic Product (GRDP), education level, average internet access, fintech loan recipient entities, and the number of mobile banking users on the dependent variable of the Financial Inclusion Index. The data was obtained from official publications of the Financial Services Authority (OJK), Bank Indonesia (BI), and the Central Statistics Agency (BPS). The results of the analysis show that Big Data and AI have a positive and significant contribution to expanding financial inclusion through increased credit distribution efficiency, expanded access to digital services, and personalized financial products. However, their influence is still limited by gaps in digital literacy, infrastructure, and trust in data security. The findings of this study are expected to provide strategic input for regulators, fintech industry players, and academics in formulating technology-based inclusive policies to achieve sustainable national financial inclusion targets.

items.title: Analyzing Applicability of Phishing Analysis and Prevention Techniques
items.abstract: Phishing protection must operate across heterogeneous attack channels, changing adversarial tactics, and stringent deployment constraints. Although recent studies report substantial gains from machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based language models, and ensemble classifiers, predictive accuracy alone does not establish whether a detector is appropriate for a particular cybersecurity setting. This article critically synthesizes fifteen peer-reviewed studies published during 2022–2026, together with authoritative authentication and e-mail security standards, to examine the applicability of conventional and artificial-intelligence-based phishing analysis and prevention techniques. A structured taxonomy distinguishes reputation and rule systems, lexical and structural URL analysis, e-mail semantics, sequence models, transformer architectures, ensembles, continual learning, and explainability mechanisms. This article introduces a context-aware applicability framework that separates minimum operational requirements from multi-criteria comparison of security efficacy, cross-source generalization, false-alarm burden, latency, resource cost, interpretability, dependency, maintainability, and preventive actionability. A reproducible evaluation protocol is specified for public URL and e-mail corpora, with safeguards against duplicate and domain leakage, temporal drift, misleading class prevalence, and incomplete end-to-end latency accounting. The evidence supports conditional rather than universal selection: inexpensive lexical models are attractive at browser and mobile endpoints; contextual text analysis adds value at e-mail gateways; and ensemble, adaptive, and explainable components are most useful when their operational overhead can be justified. The proposed defense-in-depth architecture couples detection to warnings, quarantine, phishing-resistant authentication, reporting, and incident response.

items.title: Ancestors in the machine: personhood, spirituality, and artificial intelligence - AI ethics in African cosmology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping human agency, knowledge production, decision-making, and social relations, raising ethical questions about personhood, responsibility, and technological governance. Although existing scholarship addresses relational personhood, Ubuntu, decolonial AI, indigenous knowledge, data justice, and responsible innovation, ancestral ontology and cultural memory remain comparatively underexplored in AI ethics. This study examines how African, particularly Igbo, cosmological understandings of personhood, relationality, spirituality, community, and ancestral continuity can inform ethical AI development and governance. It aims to develop an Ancestral-Relational AI Ethics Framework (AR-AIEF) that integrates African philosophical insights into contemporary debates on technological personhood and accountability. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, non-empirical philosophical design combining conceptual analysis, hermeneutical interpretation, and a critical interdisciplinary review of relevant philosophical, theological, cultural, and AI ethics literature. As a conceptual inquiry, it involves no human participants or statistical sampling. The analysis identifies relational personhood, distributed responsibility, ancestral continuity, intergenerational accountability, communal justice, and human flourishing as key principles for an African-informed approach to AI ethics. It does not equate AI systems with ancestors or attribute spirituality to machines; rather, ancestral relationality provides a lens for examining how AI stores, reproduces, simulates, and mediates cultural memory and human identity. The study contributes an African cosmological perspective to global AI ethics and recommends culturally plural governance, indigenous epistemic participation, protection of ancestral knowledge, meaningful human accountability, and intergenerationally responsible innovation. It argues that ethical AI must consider not only technological capabilities but also the communal relationships and human futures those capabilities shape.

items.title: Apex Horizon: A Dual-Theater Edge-Cloud Telemetry and Multimodal Nowcasting Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction and Agro-Forestry Resilience
items.abstract: This technical pre-print presents the operational architecture and experimental methodology of Apex Horizon, a mission-critical cyber-physical geospatial telemetry platform designed for real-time natural hazard nowcasting, environmental monitoring, and microclimate risk mitigation under degraded communication infrastructure. The system establishes an auditable multi-stream data architecture integrating open earth-observation feeds: geostationary satellite clean infrared radiometry (NOAA GOES-16 ABI and JMA Himawari-9 AHI), shortwave infrared differential fog detection (ΔTfog), synoptic aviation METAR observations, multi-source anemometer arrays, and seismic feeds. To evaluate operational robustness across distinct climatic regimes, the platform employs a dual-theater operational testbed spanning subtropical continental basins and temperate archipelago zones. Furthermore, the architecture integrates a reproducible three-tier data persistence model (relational, geospatial via PostGIS, and high-dimensional vector similarity indexing via pgvector with HNSW) to decouple raw sensor streams, upstream service trust metrics, and edge heuristic baselines. Experimental evaluation demonstrates complete telemetry preservation through an offline-first synchronization engine and resilient localized situational awareness during central backhaul outages.

items.title: APPLICATION OF PERSONALIZED AND ADAPTIVE LEARNING MODELS IN COMPUTER SCIENCE CLASSES
items.abstract: This research analyzes the application mechanisms, pedagogical significance, and upcoming challenges of personalized and adaptive learning models in computer science classes within the modern digital educational environment. Against the background of the inadequacy of traditional "one-size-fits-all" instructional methods for students with varying learning paces and prior knowledge, the role of adaptive technologies based on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and Learning Analytics is substantiated. The paper explores the positive impact of intelligent code editors, auto-graders, and dynamic adaptive testing on instructional quality, student motivation, and the development of algorithmic thinking. Simultaneously, strategic issues such as the digital divide, data privacy, and the necessity of implementing a blended learning framework are evaluated.

items.title: Argument-First Versus Language-First Generative AI Feedback in Chinese EFL Argumentative Writing: A Randomized Study
items.abstract: This eight-week randomized study examined how the order of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) feedback shaped revision and near-term independent writing among 132 Chinese English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) undergraduates. Students received argument-first (AF; n = 67) or language-first (LF; n = 65) feedback; 64 pairs underwent within-class, within-pair randomization, and four unmatched students were randomized within class. Both modules were independently generated from each initial draft (D0) and locked before release. Students completed two revisions (D1 and D2) across three tasks and a new-topic, AI-free transfer task. Adjusted AF–LF differences in D0–D2 change favored AF for overall quality (0.811 points, 95% CI [0.424, 1.198]) and argumentation (1.102 points, 95% CI [0.668, 1.536]), but not language quality (0.020 points, 95% CI [−0.381, 0.420]). Revision depth and implementation showed stage-specific crossovers. Language contrasts did not survive primary Holm adjustment, although complete-pair sensitivity analysis detected a crossover. Argumentation transfer favored AF (1.057 points, 95% CI [0.508, 1.606]); overall transfer was less consistent, with the complete-pair interval including zero (0.685 points, 95% CI [−0.111, 1.481]). Module type was structurally linked to release stage, so stage-specific contrasts describe sequence-by-stage configurations rather than isolated content or order effects. The findings support cautious use of staged feedback when argumentative development is the instructional priority.

items.title: ARIFICIAL INTELLEGENCE AND ENGLISH READING MOTIVATION INFLUENCING COMMUNICATION SKILLS AMONG PAKISTANI UNDERGRADUATE COLLEGE STUDENTS
items.abstract: The fast incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has changed how university students’ access, evaluate, produce, and communicate scientific information. At the same time, English reading motivation remains significant for Pakistani college undergraduate students because English is extensively used in academic, educational, lingua franca and scientific contexts. English language is also enjoying prestigious status in Pakistan. This study examines AI literacy and English reading motivation as predictors of science communication skills among Pakistani students. AI literacy is theorized as students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and ethically engage with AI technologies, while English reading motivation refers to students’ interest in reading for educational, academic and other purposes. Science communication skills include the skill to explain scientific concepts accurately, clearly, ethically, and appropriately to in this context with multi socio-economic and culture backgrounds of Pakistan. Existing literature suggests that AI literacy involves more than technological usage and includes critical evaluation and ethical awareness. Likewise, research on English-medium instruction indicates that language competence can influence students’ participation and learning experiences. This study has used a quantitative, correlational-predictive design involving collegiate students from Pakistani higher education institutions. Data have been collected from N=250 college students through standardized questionnaires and a science communication performance task. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression analysis have been completed. The study shows that there are evidences for assimilating AI literacy, English proficiency, and science communication into college programs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the 2027 Elections: Comparing Urban and Rural Voters' Responses to AI-Generated Campaign Messages in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18–40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1–CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and nurses’ turnover intention during healthcare digital transformation: the mediating role of occupational fatigue
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is associated with new psychological challenges. However, the extent of its impact on nursing workforce stability is unclear. Aim To explore the relationship between AI anxiety and turnover intention of clinical nurses, and the mediating effect of occupational fatigue and the moderating effect of emotional intelligence (EI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to June 2026 among 404 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Health Workers’ Occupational Fatigue Scale (HWOFS), Turnover Intention Scale (TIS) and Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS). Mediation was tested using structural equation modelling with bootstrap resampling, while moderation was tested using moderated regression analysis. Results Differences in baseline turnover intentions across age, department, and professional title level were statistically significant (all p < 0.001). Path analysis showed that AI anxiety was positively associated with occupational fatigue (β = 0.611, p < 0.001) and turnover intention (β = 0.530, p < 0.001). Occupational fatigue partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and turnover intention (indirect effect = 0.299, 95% CI: 0.129, 0.379). EI had a significant negative main effect on occupational fatigue (b = −0.257, p < 0.001), but it did not significantly moderate the association between AI anxiety and occupational fatigue. Conclusion AI anxiety is significantly correlated with the turnover intention of clinical nurses, and occupational fatigue may represent a potential pathway linking AI anxiety and turnover intention. Although EI is associated with lower levels of occupational fatigue, it fails to cushion the impact of AI anxiety, a specific stressor. Hospital administrators should focus on targeted AI literacy improvement plans and specific fatigue relief strategies to retain clinical nursing staff.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health in the Diagnosis of Leprosy: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Leprosy remains a significant public health challenge in endemic regions, where delayed diagnosis leads to irreversible nerve damage, disability, and ongoing transmission. To address the need for innovative diagnostic strategies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies have emerged as promising tools. This review explores the current applications of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and mobile health platforms in leprosy diagnosis and management. AI-based image analysis demonstrates strong potential for identifying characteristic skin lesions and differentiating leprosy from other dermatological conditions. Additionally, predictive algorithms and smartphone-based telemedicine expand access to specialized care in underserved settings while facilitating contact tracing, surveillance, and treatment monitoring. Despite these encouraging advances, significant challenges remain, including limited high-quality annotated datasets, algorithmic bias, a lack of external validation, and data privacy concerns. Ultimately, AI-driven digital health solutions should complement rather than replace clinical expertise. Prioritizing multicenter collaborations, explainable AI models, and secure data integration will be essential to strengthen global leprosy control programs, improve patient outcomes, and reduce the burden of this neglected tropical disease.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ECONOMIC SECURITY: EMERGING RISKS, GOVERNANCE CHALLENGES, AND RESILIENCE STRATEGIES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology with significant implications for economic growth, employment, financial stability, and national security. This article examines how AI reshapes economic security, understood as the capacity of households, firms, and states to withstand shocks to income, markets, and critical infrastructure. Using a structured narrative review of academic research, international policy reports, regulatory frameworks, and technical safety studies, the article identifies four principal risk domains: labor-market disruption, market concentration and infrastructure dependence, financial instability, and malicious or geopolitical misuse. The review also examines governance challenges arising from fragmented regulatory approaches, limited institutional capacity, incomplete evidence, and the rapid pace of technological deployment. The findings indicate that AI-related risks are interconnected and that vulnerabilities can spread through shared models, concentrated computing infrastructure, and correlated institutional decisions. In response, the article proposes a layered resilience framework combining adaptive regulation, competition policy, financial supervision, workforce investment, and international coordination. It concludes that economic security depends not only on preventing harmful applications of AI but also on strengthening institutions’ ability to anticipate, absorb, and recover from technological shocks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Hybrid Optimization Techniques for Non-Traditional Machining: A Comparative Review of Recent Advances and Applications
items.abstract: Non-traditional machining (NTM) processes—electrical discharge machining (EDM), electrochemical machining (ECM), laser beam machining (LBM), abrasive water jet machining (AWJM), and ultrasonic machining (USM)—are indispensable for producing geometrically intricate features in hard-to-cut super alloys, ceramics, and composites. Their governing physics are stiff, coupled, and non-stationary, making first-principles real-time control prohibitively expensive. This review surveys how machine learning surrogates—multilayer perceptron’s (MLPs), Gaussian process regression (GPR), adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS), and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)—and hybrid meta-heuristic optimizers—particle swarm optimization fused with gravitational search (PSO-GSA), and NSGA-III with reference-point decomposition—are being deployed to bridge the gap between laboratory models and shop-floor control. We present the formal governing equations for each process, compare surrogate architectures on five engineering-relevant axes, and synthesize published performance improvements across six NTM modalities in a standardized table. Critical attention is given to small-data generalization failure, the inadequacy of Ra as a surface-integrity proxy, and the architectural requirements for deploying inference on embedded FPGA/PLC controllers.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and IoT-Enabled Chemical Pollution Monitoring and Remediation of Rivers: A Comprehensive Review of Sensing Technologies, Machine Learning Methods, and IoT Integration
items.abstract: Rivers receive chemical contamination from industrial effluent, domestic sewage and agricultural runoff, including nutrients such as phosphorus, organic load, and other pollutants. Conventional assessment relies on periodic sampling and laboratory analysis, which needs specialised staff, chemicals and expertise, and therefore cannot give continuous, early warning of pollution events. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with low-cost sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT), is increasingly proposed for continuous river monitoring and for the data-driven control of chemical treatment such as coagulant dosing. This paper presents a focused narrative review of studies that use machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) with IoT sensing for river water quality monitoring and chemical-treatment control. It examines three connected themes: sensing technologies, learning methods, and IoT architectures. The reviewed literature reports water-quality classification accuracy of up to 98 % with an Arduino-based IoT device, XGBoost-based prediction in an industrially affected river basin, ML-assisted phosphorus sensing in river samples, and a deep-learning coagulant-dosing model that reduced dosage by about 22 % in a plant study. However, most studies are small, single-site, short-term and laboratory-oriented, and few report field validation, sensor fouling and drift, or closed-loop treatment control in rivers. The paper contributes a comparative table of representative studies, a conceptual river-to-decision architecture (not experimentally validated), and a prioritised list of research gaps.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics: The Future of Humanity, Mass Unemployment, Hunger, and the Global Economic Crisis
items.abstract: Abstract This working paper examines the potential economic and social consequences of accelerating artificial intelligence, robotics, and large-scale automation, with particular attention to technological unemployment, income insecurity, wealth concentration, declining purchasing power, food insecurity, and social instability. It addresses a fundamental question: What happens when machines can produce an increasing share of the goods and services humanity needs, while large numbers of people lose the employment income required to purchase those goods and services? The paper explores how automation may transform employment across agriculture, manufacturing, construction, transportation, commerce, professional services, and knowledge-based occupations. It considers the possibility that productivity gains may become increasingly concentrated among the owners of advanced technologies, while affected workers and households experience economic insecurity. Particular attention is given to developing and low-income countries, where limited household savings, informal employment, weak social protection systems, and restricted public resources may amplify the consequences of rapid technological displacement. Rather than assuming that mass unemployment, hunger, or social unrest are inevitable, the paper presents alternative future scenarios for 2036–2045 and identifies economic, institutional, and social conditions that could increase or reduce these risks. It proposes a preventive policy framework incorporating international open vocational transition institutes, proactive workforce reskilling, social funds supported by productivity and capital returns, income protection mechanisms, food security safeguards, economic early-warning indicators, and contingency plans for large-scale employment disruption. The paper calls upon researchers, governments, universities, international organizations, labor institutions, and technology companies to investigate these risks before technological displacement exceeds the capacity of societies to adapt. The central concern is not whether machines will become more productive than human beings, but whether humanity can develop economic and social institutions that ensure the benefits of technological progress remain accessible to all. This publication is an exploratory working paper and public policy proposal. It does not claim to establish a new technological discovery, present a validated economic model, or demonstrate that widespread unemployment or social crises are inevitable. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Smart Mobility Nexus: A Systematic Evidence Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping transportation through predictive analytics, intelligent infrastructure, connected mobility, autonomous systems and energy-responsive transport management. This systematic evidence review examines the AI-smart mobility nexus with an emphasis on intelligent transportation infrastructure and operational sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, 30 eligible sources published between 2015 and 2026 were synthesised from Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar. The corpus comprised 29 review, survey, meta-review, bibliometric or conceptual syntheses and one case study; accordingly, evidence was interpreted qualitatively and no pooled effect estimates were calculated. Five dominant domains emerged: AI-enabled traffic management, connected transportation infrastructure, safety and risk reduction, electric and renewable-energy-integrated mobility, and operational sustainability. Across the included literature, AI was generally associated with improved prediction, routing, incident recognition, system coordination, infrastructure monitoring and energy-management capability, although transferability depended on data quality, connectivity, infrastructure readiness, grid capacity and institutional capability. Operational efficiency did not consistently imply broader environmental or social sustainability. Interpreted through Technological Innovation Systems and Sustainability Transition perspectives, the evidence suggests that sustainable smart mobility depends on coordinated technological, infrastructural, institutional and energy-system development. The review therefore supports a qualified conclusion: AI can contribute to safer and more efficient mobility, but stronger primary, longitudinal and geographically diverse evidence is needed to establish durable environmental and social outcomes.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND VOCAL BIOMARKERS IN ASTHMA DIAGNOSIS AND MONITORING: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Considering that chronic respiratory diseases, such as asthma, represent a global challenge, their continuous monitoring is often limited by the need for specialized equipment. Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to the acoustic analysis of cough and voice emerges as a non-invasive alternative. It aims to investigate how vocal biomarkers can be isolated for the specific detection and monitoring of asthma. To this end, we proceed to a narrative review that synthesizes recent literature on the application of machine learning algorithms. In this way, it is observed that changes in respiratory mechanics modify extractable acoustic parameters, such as MFCCs. Several architectures demonstrate high accuracy, frequently exceeding 85% to 90% by fusing spectral and temporal features. Data augmentation tools overcome sample scarcity, and advanced filters mitigate ambient noise on smartphones. This allows us to conclude that AI-processed vocal biomarkers hold significant clinical potential for outpatient screening. The standardization of recording protocols and validation in multicenter cohorts are essential for the safe integration of this technology into telemedicine.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020–2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Crop Pest Detection: A Review of Deep Learning Techniques, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Pests reduce both the yield and the quality of crops, and checking fields by hand is slow, tiring, and dependent on trained experts. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly computer vision and deep learning, makes it possible to recognize pests from photographs and to respond to infestations earlier and with better precision. This review looks at AI-driven pest detection in terms of image classification, object detection, public benchmark datasets, model efficiency, and practical deployment. A focused narrative search of scholarly sources and publisher pages was carried out, covering work on the IP102 benchmark, the Pest24 dataset, machine-learning and deep-learning surveys, YOLObased pest detectors, and rice-pest detection. The literature shows that convolutional neural networks can learn the visual cues needed for pest classification, while object detectors from the YOLO family can find and label several pests within one image. The choice of dataset strongly shapes how trustworthy an evaluation is: IP102 holds more than 75,000 images in 102 categories, with bounding boxes for roughly 19,000 of them, whereas Pest24 consists of field images in which pests are small and often packed closely together. Newer model-specific studies report gains on the test sets they selected, but figures drawn from different datasets and evaluation protocols cannot be compared head to head. Challenges that keep recurring include tiny pests, look-alike species, imbalanced classes, cluttered field backgrounds, changing light, a shortage of labelled field data, and the limited computing power available on devices. The review points to the need for more representative field testing, open evaluation practices, efficient models, reporting of uncertainty, and stronger links between detection output and integrated pest management. AI-based detection is promising, yet a high benchmark score alone does not prove dependable performance on real farms. Future work should focus on external validation, ease of use for farmers, and responsible use of model predictions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Emergency Department Triage and Risk Stratification: A Review
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly investigate artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to support triage and early risk stratification in emergency departments. However, improved predictive performance does not necessarily translate into safer decisions or better patient outcomes. This critical narrative review examines the evidence for AI in adult ED care, with particular emphasis on prospective evaluation, patient safety, and clinical implementation. The review compares conventional triage systems, early warning scores, and clinician assessment with machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. It examines commonly used data inputs, prediction timing, model discrimination, calibration, external validation, and the limitations of outcome definitions. Attention is given to the distinction between predicting clinical deterioration, critical care need, short-term mortality, and hospital admission. Evidence is considered across retrospective development, external validation, silent prospective evaluation, clinician-visible implementation, and randomized trials. AI may help identify patients requiring closer assessment by integrating information from multiple sources. Nevertheless, its clinical value depends on data quality, timely predictions, generalizability, and healthcare professionals' ability to interpret outputs appropriately. Important risks include under-triage, automation bias, unequal performance across patient groups, and increased clinical workload. Prospective studies and randomized trials are therefore essential to establish whether AI-supported decisions improve patient outcomes compared with usual care. Future research should prioritize multicenter clinical evaluations, consistent outcome reporting, subgroup assessment, and continuous monitoring after deployment. AI implementation should also include clear accountability, human oversight, and procedures for reviewing adverse events. Evidence of predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to justify routine adoption. Clinical integration should depend on demonstrated safety and meaningful benefit for patients.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for facial soft‐tissue landmark localization, measurement, and classification in orthodontics: A systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract This systematic review provides a broad overview of three distinct applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in facial soft‐tissue assessment: landmark localization, automated facial measurement, and classification of soft‐tissue conditions in orthodontic and dentofacial evaluation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google Scholar, and Open Science Framework were searched. Studies using 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans, or AI‐generated facial models were included. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted QUADAS‐2 tool and certainty of evidence with GRADE. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261452521). Fifteen studies were included. Landmark‐localization performance varied substantially by imaging modality, landmark definition, data set, reference standard, and error metric; central and anatomically well‐defined landmarks were generally more accurate than peripheral or subjective points. Agreement for AI‐derived measurements ranged from poor to excellent, with ICCs of approximately 0.01–0.984. Classification accuracy ranged from approximately 0.83 to 0.98, with AUCs up to 0.98. Given only two narrowly scoped classification studies, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis‐generating rather than broadly generalizable. Because of substantial methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively. Current evidence supports AI as an adjunctive tool, but routine clinical implementation requires robust external validation and clinician oversight. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261452521

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Discovery: A Focused Review of Large Language Models for Scientific Literature, Table Understanding, and Numerical Reasoning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate scientific discovery, from predicting protein structures and molecular properties to extracting knowledge from the scientific literature. A large share of experimental evidence in papers is reported in numerical tables, yet automated analysis of such tables remains difficult. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified sources on AI for scientific discovery, concentrating on large language model (LLM) based understanding of scientific text, scientific tables and numerical reasoning. It examines three connected themes: knowledge extraction and question answering over scientific text, table question answering benchmarks, and reasoning methods (direct prompting, chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, self-consistency and graph-based reasoning). The literature shows that scientific table benchmarks have moved from mostly lookup tasks towards a 1,607-question benchmark that requires multi-step numerical reasoning; on it, GPT-4.1 mini reached only 27.0 exact match under direct prompting on the computation-and-language subset, chain-of-thought prompting raised this to 71.5, and accuracy still fell from 74.6% on small tables to 59.2% on large ones. However, the evidence is concentrated in computer science tables, depends on LLM-generated and LLM-filtered questions, and agreement among human verifiers was only moderate (Fleiss' kappa 0.55). The review contributes a comparative analysis of benchmarks and methods, a proposed conceptual architecture linking extraction, cell selection, stepwise reasoning, verification and expert review, and a prioritised list of research gaps.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
items.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Agricultural Teaching, Research, and Skill Development for Sustainable Development in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping agricultural education globally, but its integration in Nigeria remains in its early stages. This chapter focuses on systematically embedding AI into Nigeria’s agricultural education through pedagogical innovation, institutional readiness, and skills development. Instead of broadly surveying AI’s role, it critically analyzes the necessary frameworks, practices, and policies for its operational inclusion in agricultural training and research. Drawing from empirical evidence and global models (India, Kenya, Brazil, and China), the chapter explores AI-enhanced pedagogies, such as smart learning environments and digital simulations, to bolster competencies in precision agriculture, climate-smart farming, and agribusiness management. The analysis identifies four key dimensions for AI integration: curriculum redesign for competency-based learning; institutional capacity and infrastructure; ethical governance of digital systems; and alignment with Nigeria’s Digital Economy and AI Strategies. While awareness and pilot initiatives are on the rise, challenges like weak infrastructure, limited staff training, and fragmented policy implementation restrict large-scale adoption. The chapter proposes a phased integration model—encompassing awareness, capacity building, curriculum reform, and adaptive feedback—to facilitate sustainable transformation. Ultimately, it argues that AI should be regarded not just as a technological innovation but as a pedagogical framework vital for transforming Nigeria’s agricultural education ecosystem. By aligning AI with national sustainability goals, Nigeria can develop a new generation of digitally skilled, sustainability-focused agricultural professionals prepared for the challenges of the twenty-first-century food system.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in construction management: a systematic review of techniques, applications and data practices
items.abstract: Purpose This study presents an integrated systematic mapping of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in construction management, clarifying technique-domain pairings, data and validation practices, and deployment readiness across the construction lifecycle, addressing fragmentation in prior reviews. Design/methodology/approach Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidance for study identification and screening and the structured literature review approach, 148 peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2025 across 14 journals were analyzed through bibliometric and thematic synthesis. An open companion web application (https://cm.electriai.com/) was developed, providing bibliometric visualizations, a searchable paper database, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) AI assistant. Findings The review shows that AI research in construction management accelerated after 2022 but remains uneven in its technical and methodological development. Technique-domain mapping revealed lock-in patterns: vision-based deep learning (DL) was concentrated in safety, and traditional machine learning (ML) in cost estimation, while optimization, graph neural networks (GNNs), and generative AI remained underexplored. Data constraints persist: 40.5% of studies used datasets below 500 samples, 65.5% relied on private or unreported data, cross-project validation appeared in 1.4% of papers, and explainable AI (XAI) appeared in 3.4%. Practical implications Construction stakeholders require coordinated investment in open benchmark datasets, cross-project validation protocols, XAI integration and interoperable standards for building information modeling and Internet of Things systems. Originality/value This review integrates AI techniques, construction domains, data and validation practices, supported by an open companion web application for verifying, filtering, and querying the evidence base.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare and human resource management: a review of the global divide, Pakistan's landscape and institutional innovations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and organizational management worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This review examines the structural drivers of this global AI divide, situates Pakistan's healthcare and digital infrastructure challenges within this context, and presents an institutional case study of four AI-enabled interventions implemented at the Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (SIEHS), an emergency and health services organization under the Health Department, Government of Sindh, Pakistan: an AI-driven recruitment and candidate-job matching system (Talent Match Live), a facial-recognition and geolocation-based field monitoring application, an AI-assisted CCTV training-monitoring system, and an AI-augmented telemedicine triage service embedded within SIEHS's Teletabeeb telehealth department. Each intervention is evaluated against comparable systems documented in the international literature to assess feasibility, evidence of effectiveness, and associated ethical risks. A responsible-adoption framework is proposed to guide organizations in resource-constrained settings toward AI integration that is effective, equitable, and ethically governed. The review concludes that while AI offers meaningful efficiency and access gains for LMIC public-sector organizations such as SIEHS, sustainable adoption requires deliberate attention to data protection, algorithmic bias, workforce consent, and alignment with international ethical guidance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Advancing SDG 4 on Quality Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence implementation in the education field provides revolutionary methods to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning skills acquisition. This chapter assesses the strategic role of the integration of AI in the enhancement of the quality and efficiency of the post-primary education sectors. Through the adoption of the mixed research method that implies the analysis of the literature reviews and case studies, the study investigates the strategic role of AI technologies towards improved teaching practices and the effectiveness of the institutions. This study reveals the potential strategic role that AI technologies can play in reducing the gap in education access and the effective acquisition and implementation of information-based decisions in post-primary educational sectors. Through the strategic adoption of AI technologies, the study reveals the continued challenges posed by ethical approaches towards the adoption of the technologies and the implementation of equity towards capacity building. This study has proved that the adoption of AI technology in post-primary educational sectors can be an effective strategic mechanism towards the goal of SDG 4. This article Presents Recommendations on How Some of the Players Should Incorporate the AI Technologies Offered in the Enhancements of the Educational Processes Towards the SDG 4 Goals.
